The Stock dove (Columba oenas) is a cavity-nesting columbid widely distributed across temperate Eurasia, and its life-history traits reflect a balance between high adult survival and modest reproductive output. Field studies indicate that females typically produce two eggs per clutch [N_R_i = two eggs per clutch] and, under favorable conditions, initiate two clutches annually [F_R_i = two clutches annually]. At the typical body temperature of an incubating adult, measured at 40.63 °C [T = 40.63 °C], this translates to a moderate annual fecundity that is characteristic of many temperate Columbidae. The altricial nestlings emerge after a relatively short incubation period; eggs maintained at a constant temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C] during artificial incubation yield a hatching age of 16 days [ab = 16 days]. At hatching, the wet weight at birth of a newly emerged chick is approximately 12 grams [Wwb = approximately 12 grams], a value that is typical for the eggs of this species given its adult body size.

Developmental milestones under the thermal conditions typical of the active metabolic period in this species, at 40.63 °C [T = 40.63 °C], follow a predictable sequence. The young achieve sustained flight and independence from the nest at 31 days after hatching [tx = 31 days after hatching], a fledging age that is comparable to that of other hole-nesting pigeons at a temperature of 40.63 °C [T = 40.63 °C]. Puberty, defined by gonadal maturation, is attained at 93 days after hatching [tp = 93 days after hatching], meaning that a bird hatched early in the season could potentially reach reproductive readiness during its first summer at a temperature of 40.63 °C [T = 40.63 °C]. This rapid developmental trajectory enables first-year individuals to exploit seasonal peaks in food availability. The body condition and mass gain of the growing nestling are critical determinants of survival to fledging, and the species shows strong biparental care throughout the nestling and early fledgling independence period.

By the time the Stock dove reaches its ultimate wet weight, adults stabilize at a mean body mass of 291 grams [Wwi = 291 grams]. This asymptotic mass is reached by the end of the first year, after which further somatic growth is negligible. Sexual size dimorphism is minimal in this species, with both sexes converging on the same adult body mass. The attainment of this mass coincides with the completion of skeletal development and the full mineralization of flight feathers, enabling efficient long-distance foraging trips. Adult body mass in this species is somewhat lower than that of the closely related rock dove (Columba livia), consistent with the Stock dove's more dedicated reliance on natural cavities rather than anthropogenic structures for nesting. The relationship between pre-fledging mass and post-fledging survival has been documented for many columbids, and for the Stock dove, reaching the fledging mass threshold is critical for subsequent recruitment into the breeding population.

The maximum lifespan recorded for the Stock dove in the wild provides further context for interpreting its pace of life. Long-term ringing studies have documented individuals surviving as long as 12.6 years [am = 12.6 years], a longevity that is substantial for a bird of this body size operating under the thermal regime of 40.63 °C [T = 40.63 °C]. This extended lifespan, typical of many temperate columbids, is thought to buffer the species against occasional reproductive failures due to nest predation or inclement weather. The first successful brood typically occurs at 365 days after hatching [tR = 365 days after hatching], meaning that most individuals breed for the first time in the spring following their birth year at a temperature of 40.63 °C [T = 40.63 °C]. This age at first reproduction is comparatively early relative to the long potential lifespan, a combination that results in a high lifetime reproductive output when multiple annual breeding seasons are taken into account.

The Stock dove's life-history strategy is thus characterized by a moderate annual reproductive rate supported by relatively early maturation and extended adult longevity. The species is primarily granivorous, and its breeding phenology is closely tied to the availability of cereal grains and weed seeds in agricultural landscapes. Population trends in western Europe have shown declines in recent decades, largely attributed to changes in farming practices that reduce nesting cavity availability and food supply during the breeding season. Conservation efforts have focused on preserving mature hedgerow trees and providing nest boxes, which have been shown to enhance local breeding densities. From a comparative perspective, the Stock dove occupies an intermediate position among Palearctic Columbidae, displaying faster development and earlier first reproduction than the wood pigeon (Columba palumbus), yet a longer lifespan and lower annual fecundity than the smaller turtle dove (Streptopelia turtur). This suite of life-history attributes—moderate clutch size, protracted breeding season, extended adult survival, and relatively early maturation—positions Columba oenas as a typical representative of the slow–fast continuum in temperate columbids, where demographic strategies are shaped by predictable seasonal resources and cavity-nest availability.
